ApostropheCMS unauthenticated 200 OK on protected piece-type REST endpoints (CVE-2026-53609) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the post-exploitation impact of the process-wide authorization bypass: anonymous GETs to piece-type endpoints (@apostrophecms/user, @apostrophecms/global) that normally return 'notfound' (404) suddenly return 200 with paginated result bodies. Article-specific because it keys on the exact endpoints the advisory verified as bypassed and the 404→200 state change the gadget produces. Rationale: Keys on the two endpoints (@apostrophecms/user, @apostrophecms/global) the advisory explicitly verified as bypassed and the exact 404-notfound→200 behaviour change; ImWebSession's empty HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization pinpoints truly anonymous 200s. Defender/Falcon/CloudTrail/Datadog have no web-access-log surface for this server-side signal, so those fields are empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://www.thehackerwire.com/apostrophecms-critical-prototype-pollution-leads-to-auth-bypass/ • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-53609-cwe-1321-improperly-controlled-modi-874d30d1
ATT&CKT1548 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Site owner intentionally configured publicApiProjection on a piece-type, making the endpoint legitimately public (200 for anon by design)
  • Internal uptime/synthetic monitors hitting the API and receiving 200 on a genuinely public content type
  • A headless front-end SPA that reads a public piece-type via the same REST path
  • Load-balancer health checks against a public-by-config endpoint
Suppression filter
| where uri_path=="/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user"   // the user list is never legitimately public; scope alerting to it to drop public-by-config content types
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the affected endpoint (@apostrophecms/user especially) is NOT intentionally public — check the module's publicApiProjection config; a 200 to the user list from anon is never legitimate. Pull the requesting IPs and preceding PATCH activity. 2) Contain: Restart the Node.js process to clear the in-memory prototype pollution, then block offending source IPs at the WAF and force-rotate any editor credentials. 3) Hunt: Search all other piece-type endpoints for anon 200s, review the login log for the editor account that sent the poisoning PATCH, and confirm the host is upgraded to apostrophe 4.30.1.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET"
| where Url contains "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| extend st = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| where st == 200
| where isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)   // truly unauthenticated request reaching a protected piece-type endpoint
| summarize hits=count(), distinct_src=dcount(SrcIpAddr), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DstHostname, Url, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where distinct_src >= 5    // 5+ distinct anonymous clients getting 200 on a normally-404 endpoint in 5m = mass bypass
| order by LastSeen desc

ApostropheCMS $pullAll / __proto__ prototype-pollution PATCH (CVE-2026-53609) AIExploitation High
Detects the execution step: a PATCH to an ApostropheCMS piece-type doc endpoint whose body carries the prototype-pollution payload (\$pullAll, __proto__, constructor, or the publicApiProjection gadget key). Requires a body-inspecting WAF/proxy. Article-specific because it matches the exact operator (\$pullAll), traversal token (__proto__) and gadget property (publicApiProjection) named in the advisory. Rationale: Matches the advisory's literal exploit primitives — the $pullAll operator, the __proto__ traversal token, and the publicApiProjection gadget key — scoped to PATCH on /api/v1/@apostrophecms/ doc endpoints, giving a near-zero-FP WAF signature. Only a body-inspecting WAF (CommonSecurityLog) or body-logging proxy sees the payload; plain access logs (W3CIISLog/AppService) and endpoint EDR do not, hence Defender/Falcon/Datadog empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-53609-cwe-1321-improperly-controlled-modi-874d30d1
ATT&CKT1190 T1211
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security scanner (Burp, Nuclei, Nessus) probing the host with prototype-pollution test payloads
  • Internal red-team / pentest validation of the CVE
  • A developer legitimately naming a schema field 'constructor' (rare, but tokens overlap)
  • WAF in det-only mode logging the same request twice (dedup needed)
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nuclei","Nessus","masscan","zaproxy")   // drop known scanner user-agents during authorized assessments
Response runbook
1) Triage: Confirm the PATCH returned 200 (poisoning succeeded) and identify the authenticated editor token/account that sent it — the payload requires editor creds. 2) Contain: Restart the Node.js process immediately to flush the polluted Object.prototype, block the source IP, and disable/rotate the editor account used. 3) Hunt: Correlate the same source IP for subsequent anonymous 200s on piece-type endpoints (bypass validation), review WAF for additional __proto__/constructor payloads across all endpoints, and verify upgrade to 4.30.1.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH"
| where RequestURL contains "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| where RequestURL has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
    or Message has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection")
    or DeviceCustomString1 has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll")
    or DeviceCustomString2 has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceAction, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ApostropheCMS bypass chain: poisoning PATCH followed by anonymous 200 (CVE-2026-53609) AIExploitation High
Correlates the two-step exploit: a prototype-pollution PATCH (\$pullAll/__proto__) from a source IP, followed within 60s by a successful anonymous GET (200) to a protected piece-type endpoint from the same IP that previously received notfound. Higher-confidence than either event alone because it captures the attacker validating the process-wide bypass. Rationale: Ties the advisory's PoC Step 3 (poisoning PATCH with $pullAll/__proto__) to Step 4 (anonymous 200 confirming the bypass) on the same source IP within 60s — a correlated chain no benign editor workflow produces. Multi-stage temporal join, so no Sigma; WAF+proxy only, so endpoint-EDR/cloud fields empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://www.thehackerwire.com/vulnerability/CVE-2026-53609/
ATT&CKT1548 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized pentester running the full PoC end-to-end from one host
  • Automated CVE validation scanner that poisons then re-checks
  • Shared-NAT egress where an editor's PATCH and an unrelated anon reader coincidentally share a source IP within 60s (rare)
Response runbook
1) Triage: This is a high-confidence active-exploitation signal — confirm the PATCH payload and the follow-on 200, and identify the editor account tied to the poisoning request. 2) Contain: Restart the Node.js process to clear the pollution, isolate/block the attacker IP, and revoke the editor session/token. 3) Hunt: Enumerate every anonymous 200 to piece-type endpoints since PoisonTime (the bypass is process-wide, so other visitors were also exposed), assess data accessed, and confirm patch to 4.30.1.
let Poison = CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod =~ "PATCH" and RequestURL contains "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| where RequestURL has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll","publicApiProjection") or Message has_any ("__proto__","$pullAll")
| project PoisonTime=TimeGenerated, PoisonIP=SourceIP, DestinationHostName, PoisonURL=RequestURL;
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET" and toint(HttpStatusCode)==200
| where Url contains "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/" and isempty(HttpRequestHeaderAuthorization)
| join kind=inner Poison on $left.SrcIpAddr == $right.PoisonIP
| where TimeGenerated between (PoisonTime .. PoisonTime + 60s)
| extend DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', TimeGenerated, PoisonTime)
| project PoisonTime, BypassTime=TimeGenerated, AttackerIP=SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, PoisonURL, BypassURL=Url, DelaySec
| order by BypassTime desc

ApostropheCMS endpoint state flip: 404-notfound → 200 from same source (CVE-2026-53609) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Behavioral detection of the authorization-gate collapse without needing WAF body visibility: a source IP that previously received notfound (404) on a protected @apostrophecms piece-type endpoint later receives 200 on the same endpoint, with no intervening successful login. Captures the reviewer's temporal impact indicator directly from access logs. Rationale: Uses the advisory's stated gate behaviour (notfound/404 pre-exploit, paginated 200 post-exploit) as a per-source state-transition, which is visible in plain access logs even without body inspection or auth-header logging. Stateful correlation across events, so no single-event Sigma; not endpoint-EDR/cloud telemetry, so those fields empty. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-6h5j-32cf-4253 • https://radar.offseq.com/threat/cve-2026-53609-cwe-1321-improperly-controlled-modi-874d30d1
ATT&CKT1548 T1190
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A content type genuinely published/made-public between the two requests (doc newly created → legit 404 then 200)
  • publicApiProjection intentionally enabled on that piece-type after initial 404s
  • CDN/cache warming that returns 404 on a cold miss then 200 once populated
  • A client that first hit a wrong doc ID (404) then a valid one (200) on the same base path
Suppression filter
| where uri_path=="/api/v1/@apostrophecms/user"   // restrict to the never-public user endpoint to eliminate content-publish 404→200 noise
Response runbook
1) Triage: Focus on the /user endpoint flips first (never legitimately public); confirm no config/deploy change or content-publish event explains the 404→200. 2) Contain: If unexplained, restart the Node.js process to clear pollution and block the source; capture the request window for forensics. 3) Hunt: Look for a preceding editor PATCH with $pullAll/__proto__ on the same host, count how many distinct anonymous sources subsequently got 200s, and verify the instance is on 4.30.1.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2d)
| where HttpMethod =~ "GET" and Url contains "/api/v1/@apostrophecms/"
| extend st = toint(HttpStatusCode)
| where st in (200,404)
| summarize first404=minif(TimeGenerated, st==404), first200=minif(TimeGenerated, st==200), total=count() by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname, Url
| where isnotempty(first404) and isnotempty(first200) and first200 > first404   // same source flips from blocked(404) to allowed(200) on the same protected endpoint
| extend FlipDelaySec = datetime_diff('second', first200, first404)
| order by first200 desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| eval t404=if(status="404",_time,null()), t200=if(status="200",_time,null())

Internet-exposed ApostropheCMS instance inventory for CVE-2026-53609 exposure AIReconnaissance Low
Discovery/asset hunt: inventories hosts serving the ApostropheCMS piece-type REST API (/api/v1/@apostrophecms/*) so the SOC can cross-reference internet-facing instances against the vulnerable version range (apostrophe ≤ 4.30.0, patched 4.30.1). Atomic Arch AUR loader/stealer known-bad file & process hashes AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution or on-disk presence of the July 2026 AUR (openconnect-sso) two-stage loader and Rust infostealer by their published SHA256/MD5 hashes. Article-specific: these hashes belong to the IFIN-analyzed Atomic Arch campaign redistributed through hijacked AUR package adoptions. Rationale: Uses the four campaign SHA256 hashes plus the MD5 pre-extracted from the article; SHA256 6144d433... is independently confirmed as the Rust stealer binary by The Hacker News and GuardSix, so hash-based matching is high-fidelity with near-zero FP. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://discourse.ifin.network/t/new-aur-attack-prompts-adoption-lock/698
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Malware analyst detonating the sample in an authorized sandbox that reports to production EDR
  • Threat-intel/VirusTotal retrohunt downloads of the sample onto a research host
  • Incident-response tooling copying the artifact for evidence collection
  • Backup/AV quarantine re-scanning a previously captured copy
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("clamscan","freshclam","vt","virustotal") and FolderPath !has "/quarantine/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the host is Arch/Arch-based and whether any AUR package (openconnect-sso, boringssl-git, icloudpd, windscribe-cli-v2-bin, stirling-pdf-desktop-bin, pgadmin4-server) was recently installed/updated via makepkg. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the matching PID, and treat all local secrets (SSH keys, browser creds, cloud/dev/AI tokens) as compromised. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, systemd units with Restart=always, and cron entries; rotate SSH keys and check known_hosts targets for lateral spread.

Tor client masquerading as dbus-daemon making external network connections AICommand & Control High
Hunts the Atomic Arch first-stage behaviour of launching a Tor client renamed to 'dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion C2. A legitimate dbus-daemon is a local IPC bus and never initiates public/internet egress, so any outbound public connection from a dbus-daemon process is high-fidelity. Rationale: Article states the loader 'downloads and launches a Tor client disguised as dbus-daemon' to reach an .onion server; corroborated by GuardSix noting C2 via a Tor onion service. dbus-daemon making public egress (Defender/Falcon) or running outside /usr/bin (Sentinel/Datadog/Sigma) is essentially never legitimate. Cross-checked against: • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1036.005 T1573.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom-built dbus deployed to a non-standard prefix (/usr/local/bin) on developer boxes — path variant only
  • D-Bus remote/TCP transport intentionally configured in a container or CI runner
  • Chaos/network-testing tooling renamed to system binaries during red-team exercises
  • Flatpak/snap sandboxes shipping their own dbus-daemon under /app or /snap paths
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !in~ ("/usr/bin","/usr/local/bin") or RemotePort in (9001, 9030, 9050, 443)
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full path, hash, and command line of the dbus-daemon process; a real one lives at /usr/bin/dbus-daemon and only talks to unix sockets — confirm the destination IP/port and whether it looks like a Tor guard node (443/9001). 2) Contain: isolate the host and kill the process; block the destination IP at egress. 3) Hunt: locate the parent AUR build (makepkg), the second-stage stealer under /var/lib or ~/.config, and any systemd/cron persistence; rotate all secrets on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "dbus-daemon"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), RemoteIPs = make_set(RemoteIP, 25) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has "dbus-daemon"
| where TargetProcessName !has "/usr/bin/dbus-daemon"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Non-package-manager process writing systemd unit or cron persistence (Atomic Arch) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the loader's persistence step: writing a systemd service (Restart=always) to /etc/systemd/system or ~/.config/systemd/user, plus cron jobs, from a process that is NOT a package manager or systemctl. Article-specific to the AUR loader installing systemd services and cron jobs after anti-analysis checks. Rationale: Article states the loader 'installs systemd services and cron jobs to ensure persistence'; StepSecurity/GuardSix confirm a Restart=always unit dropped to /etc/systemd/system (root) or ~/.config/systemd/user (user). Keying on non-package-manager writers to these exact paths captures the malicious writer while excluding legit installs to /usr/lib/systemd/system. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign • https://guardsix.com/blog/atomic-arch-zombie-package-apocalypse
ATT&CKT1543.002 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin hand-authoring a unit with a text editor (vim/nano) or writing crontab via a script
  • Configuration management (Ansible/Chef/Puppet/Salt) deploying systemd units or cron jobs
  • Developer enabling a user service under ~/.config/systemd/user for a legitimate app
  • Container build steps or dotfile-management tools writing unit files
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("ansible","ansible-playbook","puppet","chef-client","salt-minion","vim","nano","vi","tee") and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("ansible","puppet","chef","salt"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the dropped unit/cron file — malicious ones point ExecStart at a binary under /var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp or /dev/shm and use Restart=always; benign ones point at packaged binaries in /usr/bin. 2) Contain: disable/remove the unit or cron entry, kill the referenced binary, and isolate the host if the target is a non-package path. 3) Hunt: pivot to the writing process's ancestry (makepkg build?), check for the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process and stealer artifacts, and rotate host secrets.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has_any ("/.config/systemd/user/","/etc/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/")
| where FileName endswith ".service" or FolderPath has "cron"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("systemctl","systemd","pacman","dpkg","apt","apt-get","rpm","dnf","yum","install","crontab")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRename")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("/.config/systemd/user/","/etc/systemd/system/","/etc/cron.d/","/var/spool/cron/")
| where TargetFilePath endswith ".service" or TargetFilePath has "cron"
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("systemctl","systemd","pacman","dpkg","apt","rpm","dnf","crontab"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SSH worm: persistence-path binary spawning ssh/scp for self-propagation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the Atomic Arch stealer's SSH worm capability — a binary running from a malware persistence directory (/var/lib, ~/.config, /tmp, /dev/shm) spawning ssh/scp/sftp/rsync to copy and execute itself on other hosts using stolen SSH keys. Distinguishes malware-driven lateral movement from interactive/administrative SSH. Rationale: Article states the stealer 'can spread laterally by using stolen SSH keys to copy and execute itself on other systems'; corroborated by StepSecurity/HackerNews noting SSH-key and known_hosts theft. Anchoring on ssh/scp spawned by a parent living in the confirmed persistence directories (/var/lib for root, ~/.config for user) targets the worm rather than routine admin SSH. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/400-aur-packages-hijacked-atomic-arch-campaign
ATT&CKT1021.004 T1552.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom deployment/orchestration scripts installed under /var/lib or a user's ~/.config wrapper that call scp/rsync
  • CI/CD runner or backup agent staged in /tmp or /var/lib performing rsync-over-ssh
  • Developer helper tools in ~/.config invoking git-over-ssh (partly excluded via git filter)
  • Config-management agents copying files to fleet hosts over ssh
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("ansible","rsnapshot","borg","restic","rclone") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("gitlab-runner","buildkite-agent","jenkins")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect the parent binary's path, hash, and the ssh/scp command line — note the destination host/user and whether a copy of the parent binary is being transferred. 2) Contain: isolate the source host, kill the process, and pre-emptively isolate the destination host(s) named in the command line; revoke/rotate the SSH keys used. 3) Hunt: on each destination host, hunt for the same persistence (systemd Restart=always, cron), the disguised dbus-daemon Tor process, and the campaign hashes; expand outward via known_hosts entries.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("ssh","scp","sftp","rsync")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("git","ansible","ansible-playbook","bash","sh","zsh","fish","rsync","ssh","code")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("/ssh","/scp","/sftp","/rsync")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/var/lib/","/tmp/","/.config/","/dev/shm/")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("/git","/ansible","/bash","/sh","/zsh","/fish","/rsync","/ssh"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Persistence-Path Binary Spawning SSH/SCP for Propagation (Atomic Arch Worm)
id: d7b3f981-2c44-4a90-9e15-3b8c6a1f2e57
description: Detects ssh/scp/sftp/rsync spawned by a parent process located in a malware persistence directory, matching the Atomic Arch stealer's SSH-worm self-propagation.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/arch-linux-disables-aur-package-adoption-to-stop-malware-flood/
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/over-400-arch-linux-aur-packages.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/08/01
tags:
  - attack.t1021.004
  - attack.t1552.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/ssh'
      - '/scp'
      - '/sftp'
      - '/rsync'
    ParentImage|contains:
      - '/var/lib/'
      - '/tmp/'
      - '/.config/'
      - '/dev/shm/'
  filter:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '/git'
      - '/ansible'
      - '/bash'
      - '/sh'
      - '/zsh'
      - '/fish'
  condition: selection and not filter
level: medium
source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(scp OR rsync OR sftp) @process.command_line:(*/var/lib/* OR */dev/shm/* OR */.config/*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| ImageFileName=/\/(ssh|scp|sftp|rsync)$/i
| ParentImageFileName=/(\/var\/lib\/|\/tmp\/|\/\.config\/|\/dev\/shm\/)/i
| NOT ParentBaseFileName=/(git|ansible|bash|sh|zsh|fish|rsync|ssh)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentImageFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("ssh","scp","sftp","rsync")) (Processes.parent_process_path IN ("*/var/lib/*","*/tmp/*","*/.config/*","*/dev/shm/*")) NOT (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("git","ansible","bash","sh","zsh","fish","rsync","ssh")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_path Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("ssh","scp","sftp","rsync")) (Processes.parent_process_path IN ("*/var/lib/*","*/tmp/*","*/.config/*","*/dev/shm/*")) NOT (Processes.parent_process_name IN ("git","ansible","bash","sh","zsh","fish","rsync","ssh")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process_path Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control

    category: process_creation
    product: windows

        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'
            - '\TeamViewer.exe'

            - '\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe'
            - '\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe'

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

DeviceNetworkEvents

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or SHA1 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502") or MD5 in~ ("e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["e73a35b3e75e94746428d1a207703d6335933deadee7d1d9c9d0328df7b9df77", "2d25d2ea313767fae5808164224cf6ad610ab09546d1e5a6f033eedbfd98a281", "06c857c8ca798d50c765b4de39e6c4f272ecb57bc8316a8ed4c0fdf02fb59502"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process_hash

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Online ad firm Adform’s script compromised to steal cryptocurrency
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match

C2 beacon to Adform clipper attacker server 84.32.102.230:7744 AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to the attacker-controlled server (84.32.102.230, port 7744) that the trojanized Adform scripts beaconed to, exfiltrating victim IP, referring website and URL path. Any host reaching this IP indicates a browser that loaded the compromised trackpoint-async.js during the July 2026 supply-chain window. Rationale: 84.32.102.230:7744 is the attacker-controlled C2 confirmed in both Beaumont's DoublePulsar analysis and BleepingComputer; it is not owned by Adform and has no benign use, making any connection a high-fidelity indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1195.002 T1115
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher or malware sandbox intentionally detonating the IOC
  • Threat-intel scanner/crawler validating the C2 from an internal host
  • IP later reassigned to a benign shared-hosting tenant (verify port 7744 and date window July 2026)
  • Corporate VPN/proxy egress IP coincidentally matching (unlikely - it's a /32 attacker host)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the host, user and initiating process for the connection; confirm it is a browser (chrome.exe/msedge.exe/firefox.exe) and whether the timestamp falls in the 26-27 July 2026 window. 2) Contain: block 84.32.102.230 at firewall/proxy, and if repeated beaconing is seen, isolate the host and force browser cache/cookie clearing per Adform's guidance. 3) Hunt: pivot to all other hosts that touched this IP, warn affected users to re-verify any crypto wallet addresses they copied/pasted recently, and check for the malicious script hash (see companion UC).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationIP == "84.32.102.230"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, SourceUserName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Compromised Adform trackpoint-async.js clipper script by SHA256 on endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Retro-hunts the fleet for the exact malicious trojanized Adform tracking library (SHA256 02ff86c7...) landing on disk, typically as a browser cache artifact, to scope which endpoints downloaded the crypto-clipper during the supply-chain window. VirusTotal flagged this file clean across all engines, so hash-based hunting is required rather than AV signal. Rationale: SHA256 02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55 is the pre-extracted hash of the injected library; because VirusTotal shows zero detections, an exact-hash file hunt is the only reliable way to scope endpoint exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://doublepulsar.com/adform-compromised-to-serve-crypto-stealer-via-supply-chain-attack-2f1ec024f33e • https://www.it-connect.tech/adform-breach-ad-script-steals-cryptocurrency-for-at-least-a-week/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1115 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A DFIR analyst intentionally saving the sample to an endpoint for analysis
  • A copy of the sample pulled from Beaumont's Pastebin/Archive.org for internal review
  • Malware-repo or IOC-feed clone stored on a workstation
  • SHA256 collision (cryptographically negligible - treat any exact match as true positive)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the file path (browser cache dir vs a saved copy) and the FileOriginUrl/downloading process to distinguish a real infection from analyst handling. 2) Contain: on genuine infections, clear the affected browser's cache/cookies as Adform advises, block 84.32.102.230, and advise the user to re-check any crypto addresses copied on 26-27 July 2026. 3) Hunt: correlate matching hosts against the C2-beacon UC, and search proxy logs for retrievals of trackpoint-async.js from s2.adform.net/a1.adform.net/ai1.adform.net during the window to build the full impacted-user list.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA256 == "02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or SHA1 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55") or MD5 in~ ("02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["02ff86c7f9fe609a753ff15bda90baa3c3e0d4a2e559ec4fcf8a3de0954b7c55"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-31 18 use cases 15 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Storm-2945, a sub-cluster of the Russian threat actor Midnight Blizzard, has been observed compromising the sign-in portals of hospitality-related organizations such as hotels since May 2026 in order to deliver malware to travelers and steal credentials in an operation we call CaptiveCrunch. The post CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware delivery and credential theft appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1047 T1053.005 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1190 T1204.002 T1204.004 T1218.005 T1218.011 T1528 T1539 T1547.001 T1555.003

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Captive-portal hijack: connectivity-check endpoint resolving to Storm-2945 IP · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] ClickFix fake-update chain: browser/Run-dialog interpreter reaching Storm-2945 infra · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — CaptiveCrunch: Midnight Blizzard targets travelers worldwide for malware deliver
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CornFlake implant execution from %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe · [LLM] CornFlake persistence: 'svchost32' service / 'Cloud Sync Service' registration · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Network connection to Storm-2945 doppelganger M365 domains / C2 IPs · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Entra sign-in / device-code auth from Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch IPs · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
CornFlake implant execution from %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of Storm-2945's CornFlake Go RAT, which drops itself to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe and runs from there to masquerade as the legitimate svchost.exe. The nested svchost32\svchost32.exe path is a unique CaptiveCrunch artifact. Rationale: Anchored on the exact CornFlake drop path %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe from the article body and code block 3 — no legitimate binary runs from a svchost32\svchost32.exe subfolder. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://cyberinsider.com/hackers-use-dns-poisoning-on-hotel-wi-fi-to-steal-microsoft-365-accounts/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A poorly-named internal tool that happens to install to an AppData\svchost32 folder (extremely rare)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sandbox/lab image
  • EDR test/atomic-red-team simulation copying a binary to that exact path
  • Backup/imaging tools restoring an already-infected user profile
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SHA256 of svchost32.exe, confirm it is not a signed Microsoft binary and check InitiatingProcess (should trace back to a browser/fake-update download). 2) Contain: isolate the device in Defender, kill/quarantine %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe, disable the svchost32 service and any matching Run key/scheduled task. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device to DeviceNetworkEvents for the Storm-2945 domains/IPs, and check Entra sign-ins from the same user for device-code registration.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, ReportId
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\svchost32\svchost32.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine, NewProcessId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CornFlake persistence: 'svchost32' service / 'Cloud Sync Service' registration AIInstallation High
Detects CornFlake registering its Windows service named svchost32 with display name 'Cloud Sync Service' and description 'Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider'. These exact service metadata strings are unique to the CaptiveCrunch implant. Rationale: Uses the article's verbatim service name (svchost32), display name ('Cloud Sync Service') and description string ('Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider') — none of which collide with genuine Windows services. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1036.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate third-party cloud-sync product coincidentally using an svchost32 service name (not observed in the wild)
  • Red-team persistence emulation using the published CaptiveCrunch service metadata
  • Restoration of an infected system image that re-registers the service
  • Analyst manually re-creating the service during malware analysis
Response runbook
1) Triage: read ImagePath/ServiceFileName — confirm it points to %APPDATA%\svchost32\svchost32.exe rather than %SystemRoot%\System32\svchost.exe. 2) Contain: stop and delete the svchost32 service (sc delete), isolate the host, quarantine the binary. 3) Hunt: enumerate the host's Run keys and scheduled tasks for redundant persistence (article notes multiple mechanisms + a watchdog) and sweep the fleet for the same ServiceName.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\svchost32"
   or (RegistryValueName == "DisplayName" and RegistryValueData =~ "Cloud Sync Service")
   or (RegistryValueName == "Description" and RegistryValueData =~ "Synchronizes files with the cloud storage provider")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID in (4697, 7045)
| where ServiceName =~ "svchost32" or ServiceFileName has "svchost32"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Network connection to Storm-2945 doppelganger M365 domains / C2 IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on any host contacting the CaptiveCrunch adversary infrastructure — the four Microsoft-lookalike domains and six C2 IPs published by Microsoft and corroborated by ReliaQuest. Direct IOC match against Storm-2945 AiTM/phishing and malware C2 nodes. Rationale: Straight IOC match on the four doppelganger domains and six IPs from the article's code block 2, independently corroborated by ReliaQuest's report on the same ms365-live.com device-code infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://gbhackers.com/hotel-wi-fi-dns-poisoning-attacks/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel/DNS sinkhole platforms actively resolving the IOCs for enrichment
  • Security tooling detonating samples that beacon to these nodes in a lab
  • A researcher browsing to the phishing pages for analysis
  • Stale passive-DNS crawlers hitting the domains
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process — a browser indicates AiTM phishing, an interpreter/svchost32.exe indicates active C2. 2) Contain: block all four domains and six IPs at proxy/firewall/DNS, isolate any host that connected. 3) Hunt: for connecting users, review Entra SigninLogs for successful auth from the same IPs and any new device registrations; sweep the fleet for CornFlake persistence artifacts.

| where RemoteUrl has_any(target_domains) or RemoteIP in (target_ips)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

Captive-portal hijack: connectivity-check endpoint resolving to Storm-2945 IP AIDelivery Medium
Detects CaptiveCrunch traffic manipulation where OS/browser connectivity-check (NCSI) endpoints such as msftconnecttest.com or captive.apple.com resolve to Storm-2945 C2 IPs — the mechanism used to serve fake browser/OS 'updates'. Correlating the NCSI hostname with an attacker IP is a very high-fidelity captive-portal-compromise signal. Rationale: Combines the connectivity-check endpoint list from code block 1 with the six C2 IPs from code block 2 — an NCSI host answering with attacker IP space is a direct fingerprint of the captive-portal DNS/HTTP manipulation described, with essentially no benign explanation. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/hotel-wifi-dns-poisoning/
ATT&CKT1557 T1189
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A misconfigured internal split-DNS answering NCSI names with private/overlapping addresses (won't match the public attacker IPs, but flag if IOC IPs get reused)
  • Threat-intel lab replaying pcap of the campaign
  • A captive-portal appliance vendor legitimately intercepting NCSI for its own portal (validate the answering IP is not Storm-2945 space)
  • Passive-DNS sensor logging historical poisoned records
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the answering IP is one of the six Storm-2945 nodes and note which network/SSID the device was on (likely hotel/conference Wi-Fi). 2) Contain: instruct the user to disconnect from that Wi-Fi and enforce full-tunnel VPN; check the device for a fake-update download and CornFlake artifacts. 3) Hunt: review the user's Entra sign-ins for device-code auth from the same time window and sweep other travelers on the same venue network.

let target_ips = dynamic(["31.57.243.154","38.146.28.75","38.146.28.132","104.194.159.150","107.189.26.194","213.145.86.112"]);

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

Entra sign-in / device-code auth from Storm-2945 CaptiveCrunch IPs AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects successful Microsoft Entra authentication originating from the six Storm-2945 C2 IPs — the identity-plane side of the AiTM device-code phishing that harvests M365 tokens from traveling corporate users. Directly targets the token-theft objective of CaptiveCrunch. Rationale: Uses the six confirmed Storm-2945 IPs against the Entra sign-in plane; ReliaQuest independently confirms device-code OAuth token theft via this same infrastructure (ms365-live.com), making a successful auth from these IPs a token-compromise indicator. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/02/13/storm-2372-conducts-device-code-phishing-campaign/
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1528 T1621
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A corporate egress/VPN concentrator that coincidentally shares an IP range with an IOC (validate exact /32 match)
  • Security team replaying captured tokens in a controlled purple-team exercise
  • Threat-intel enrichment services authenticating test accounts
  • A user on a compromised hotel network whose benign traffic egresses via the same node (still worth investigating)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user and app/resource authenticated to (watch for 'Microsoft Authentication Broker' / Device Registration Service = device-code registration). 2) Contain: revoke the user's refresh tokens and sessions (revokeSignInSessions), require password reset + re-MFA, remove any attacker-registered device from Entra. 3) Hunt: pull Graph/OfficeActivity for mailbox access or bulk mail download by that identity, and check for the same IPs across other users.

ClickFix fake-update chain: browser/Run-dialog interpreter reaching Storm-2945 infra AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CaptiveCrunch ClickFix delivery where a browser- or explorer-spawned script interpreter (the Run-dialog paste / fake-update click) makes an outbound request to Storm-2945 domains/IPs to pull the CornFlake payload. Ties user-execution of the ClickFix lure to confirmed C2 infrastructure. Rationale: Models the article's ClickFix fake-update flow (browser/Run-dialog -> interpreter -> payload download) and raises fidelity by pinning the download target to the confirmed Storm-2945 domains/IPs in the Defender/Falcon variants; the .apk token covers the noted Android landing. Cross-checked against: • https://reliaquest.com/blog/threat-spotlight-dns-poisoning-tactics-expand-to-hospitality/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT scripts launched by users double-clicking a .cmd/.ps1 from Explorer that fetch internal resources over HTTP
  • Browser-integrated updaters or extensions invoking curl/bitsadmin to legitimate CDNs
  • Developers running curl/Invoke-WebRequest from a file-manager-spawned shell
  • Software deployment tools staged from Downloads and executed via Explorer
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "\\\\corp\\" and RemoteIPType == "Public"
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full interpreter command line and the RemoteUrl/RemoteIP — a Storm-2945 domain/IP is a confirmed hit; otherwise assess the download target reputation. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the URL/IP, capture and quarantine any dropped payload (check %APPDATA%\svchost32). 3) Hunt: correlate to a preceding captive-portal NCSI redirect (UC 'Captive-portal hijack') and to CornFlake persistence, and confirm whether the user was on external/hotel Wi-Fi.

| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe")

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject

Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] NocoBase anonymous account signup via auth-basic allowSignUp · [LLM] NocoBase signup immediately followed by myInAppChannels access from same IP
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] CVE-2026-52887 SQLi payload in NocoBase myInAppChannels latestMsgReceiveTimestamp filter

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PostgreSQL server process spawning a shell (COPY TO PROGRAM RCE in DB container) · Article-specific behavioural hunt — [GHSA / CRITICAL] CVE-2026-52887: NocoBase: SQL injection in /api/myInAppChannel
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PostgreSQL process making outbound public network connection (post-RCE egress)
NocoBase anonymous account signup via auth-basic allowSignUp AIDelivery Medium
Hunts successful POST requests to NocoBase's /api/auth:signUp endpoint, the anonymous foothold that CVE-2026-52887 depends on because the myInAppChannels SQLi is gated only by the 'loggedIn' ACL. Surfaces external clients self-registering member accounts on an internet-facing NocoBase instance. Rationale: Uses the exact NocoBase resource:action route '/api/auth:signUp' with POST+200 named in the article's reproduction step 1; a 200 here means an account was minted with no admin involvement. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/nocobase/nocobase/security/advisories/GHSA-4948-f92q-f432 • https://www.sentinelone.com/vulnerability-database/cve-2026-41641/
ATT&CKT1190 T1136.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate open-registration NocoBase tenants where public signup is an intended feature
  • Marketing/demo instances that expose signup for trial users
  • QA/automation harnesses creating test accounts against staging
  • Security scanners (internal pentest) registering accounts
Suppression filter
| where DstHostname !in~ ("demo.internal.example","trial.example")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the target host is a production NocoBase instance that should NOT allow public signup; pull the source IP/ASN and check for burst of signups. 2) Contain: disable allowSignUp in the auth-basic authenticator (set allowSignUp:false) and disable/delete the newly created member accounts; block the source IP at the WAF. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same SrcIpAddr for follow-on /api/myInAppChannels:list requests within minutes (see chain UC) and for auth:signIn events that yielded a member JWT.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url has "/api/auth:signUp"
| where HttpMethod =~ "POST"
| where HttpStatusCode in ("200","201")
| summarize Signups = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), UserAgents = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 10) by SrcIpAddr, DstHostname
| order by Signups desc
