Ruby/Puma Rails web process spawns a shell (post-file-read RCE via forged secret_key_base cookie) AIExploitation Medium
Detects the RCE stage of CVE-2026-66066: after leaking secret_key_base, the attacker forges a signed/encrypted Rails cookie carrying a deserialization payload, yielding code execution inside the app process. Surfaces the anomalous child — an interactive shell or download tool spawned by the Ruby/Puma web worker. Rationale: The advisory states the file-read escalates to RCE via secrets in the process environment; the observable outcome is the Rails worker (ruby/puma/passenger) spawning a shell or fetch tool — a parent→child pair that is abnormal for a web app running the in-process :vips processor. Parents and children are all concrete binary names, no placeholders. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm • https://blog.flatt.tech/entry/kindarails2shell_rails
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1190 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rails apps that legitimately shell out via system()/backticks (e.g. running git, imagemagick/mini_magick, ffmpeg, or a rake task)
  • Deploy/boot scripts where puma is launched by a shell wrapper and re-execs sh
  • Health-check or cron jobs invoking curl/wget from within the app container
  • Background job workers (Sidekiq/Resque under ruby) shelling out to CLI tools by design
  • Container entrypoints where bundle exec spawns sh for pre-boot hooks
Suppression filter
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/dev/tcp","-i ","sh -c","bash -c","-c 'curl","-c \"curl","base64 -d") or ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("git","convert","mogrify","ffmpeg","rake")
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect ProcessCommandLine of the child — reverse-shell markers (/dev/tcp, -i, bash -c with piped curl) or interactive shells with no args are high-confidence; benign shell-outs name a specific tool/arg. Correlate against UC1 file-read hits on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host/pod, kill the offending Ruby worker, and rotate secret_key_base + all env-resident credentials (the RCE path depends on the leaked signing key). 3) Hunt: pull the preceding web requests to /rails/active_storage/representations/ and /rails/active_storage/direct_uploads, review outbound connections from the host, and check for persistence (cron, authorized_keys, new services).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ruby","ruby3.2","ruby3.3","puma","passenger","bundle","rails")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","nc","ncat","curl","wget","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessId
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("ruby","puma","passenger","bundle","rails")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("/sh","/bash","/dash","/zsh","/nc","/ncat","/curl","/wget","/python","/perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Internet-facing hosts running activestorage vulnerable to CVE-2026-66066 AIExploitation High
Exposure hunt for the attack surface: hosts with an activestorage version affected by CVE-2026-66066 (< 7.2.3.2, 8.0.x < 8.0.5.1, 8.1.x < 8.1.3.1), prioritising internet-facing systems and those still on libvips < 8.13 which cannot block unfuzzed loaders. Drives patch/mitigation before the 2026-08-28 full disclosure. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and the vendor-published affected-version boundaries from the advisory; joining internet-facing status turns a raw inventory list into a ranked remediation queue for the specific gem in this CVE. No version-string math needed — the TVM CveId already encodes the affected ranges. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-xr9x-r78c-5hrm
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Hosts already patched to 7.2.3.2 / 8.0.5.1 / 8.1.3.1 but TVM inventory not yet refreshed (stale)
  • Apps that carry ruby-vips only for image analysis and never generate variants (lower real risk despite matching)
  • Hosts where libvips >= 8.13 is present and VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED / Vips.block_untrusted(true) is already set (mitigated without gem upgrade)
  • Non-production/staging boxes flagged as internet-facing by network heuristics but actually firewalled
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit confirm variant_processor is :vips (default since load_defaults 7.0) and whether the app accepts uploads from untrusted users — those two conditions gate real exploitability. 2) Contain: upgrade activestorage to the fixed release and ensure libvips >= 8.13; where an immediate upgrade isn't possible, set VIPS_BLOCK_UNTRUSTED=1 (or Vips.block_untrusted(true)) as an interim block, prioritising internet-facing hosts. 3) Hunt: on any host that was exposed before patching, assume secret exposure — rotate secret_key_base, master.key, DB and Active Storage service credentials, and run UC1/UC2 retrospectively over the exposure window.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-66066"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc, DeviceName asc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-66066"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d) | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, DeviceId, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, RecommendedSecurityUpdate, IsInternetFacing, OSPlatform
| order by IsInternetFacing desc

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities

DPRK-Linked macOS Malvertising Uses Fake Updates to Deliver Crypto-Stealing Malware

The Hacker News
2026-07-30 20 use cases 13 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

A lot of security still comes down to trusting the wrong screen. This week, that screen might be a login page, an install guide, a recruiter call, or a familiar service behaving slightly wrong. Behind it: reused credentials, exposed systems, quiet loaders, abused trust, and exploit paths that should have been harder. Some defenses improved. The loose parts still got found first. Anyway,

ClickFix rundll32 ordinal (#1) execution of non-DLL payload over WebDAV @SSL AIExploitation High
Hunts the CyberProof-tracked ClickFix variant where a pasted Run-dialog command mounts an attacker WebDAV share (\\host@SSL\GUID) and uses rundll32.exe to load a non-DLL file (gc.key, j.pm, goog.ct) by ordinal export #1. Article-specific because it keys on the payload filenames plus the rundll32 ',#1' + '@SSL' WebDAV UNC combination rather than generic rundll32 abuse. Rationale: Keys on the three verbatim payload filenames (gc.key/j.pm/goog.ct) and the rundll32 ',#1' ordinal-load plus '@SSL' WebDAV UNC syntax quoted in the CyberProof write-up — a combination that does not occur in benign rundll32 usage, which always references a real .dll by exported name. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyberproof.com/blog/clickfix-keeps-evolving-rundll32-ordinal-execution-over-webdav/ • https://gbhackers.com/rundll32-and-webdav/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/new-clickfix-variant-uses-rundll32/
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1204.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate software installers that call rundll32 with a real DLL export happen to contain the literal token '#1' in an unrelated argument (rare — no @SSL/payload-name overlap)
  • Internal red-team / purple-team ClickFix simulations reusing the public payload names
  • Security tooling detonating the sample in a sandbox that shares the production Defender workspace
  • A file share genuinely named with '@SSL' in its path (uncommon; WebDAV-over-HTTPS UNC is almost never used interactively)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe") and ProcessCommandLine !has "@SSL" and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("gc.key","j.pm","goog.ct"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full ProcessCommandLine and parent chain (explorer.exe->powershell/pcalua/cmd->rundll32). Extract the WebDAV host from the '\\host@SSL' UNC and the payload filename; check DeviceNetworkEvents for the 443/WebDAV connection to that host. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, block the WebDAV domain at proxy/DNS, and kill/quarantine any child processes rundll32 spawned. Reset the user's credentials if hands-on-keyboard follow-on is seen. 3) HUNT: Sweep the org for rundll32 loading any non-.dll file by ordinal '#1', for WebClient service starts, and for the same WebDAV domains across all endpoints; review clipboard/Run-dialog (RunMRU) history on the victim.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "#1"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("gc.key", "j.pm", "goog.ct") or ProcessCommandLine has "@SSL"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
| where CommandLine has "#1"
| where CommandLine has_any ("gc.key", "j.pm", "goog.ct") or CommandLine has "@SSL"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MacSync fake-Claude Terminal one-liner: curl piped to zsh via base64 -D AIDelivery High
Hunts the Huntress-documented MacSync initial-access step where a victim pastes a Terminal one-liner (curl -kfsSL $(echo <b64>|base64 -D)|zsh) that resolves to agenticsora[.]com or malwareaudit[.]com /curl/<token> and executes the stage-1 zsh loader. Article-specific because it pins on the exact delivery domains and the base64-decode-then-pipe-to-zsh shape rather than generic curl usage. Rationale: Uses the two verbatim delivery domains (agenticsora[.]com, malwareaudit[.]com) from the Huntress reversing plus the distinctive 'curl ... $(...|base64 -D)|zsh' construction — legitimate macOS install guides fetch signed .dmg/.pkg files, they do not base64-decode a URL and pipe HTTP to the shell. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://cybersecuritynews.com/fake-claude-code-install-guide/ • https://gbhackers.com/fake-claude-code-installer-3/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.004 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using curl|zsh for a trusted install script (e.g. Homebrew, oh-my-zsh) — excluded by the domain/base64-decode anchors
  • Internal macOS provisioning tooling that pipes remote scripts to a shell (should not reference the attacker domains)
  • Security researcher intentionally detonating the MacSync sample
  • CI runners on macOS fetching bootstrap scripts (won't match the specific domains or the base64 -D wrapper)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("brew.sh", "raw.githubusercontent.com", "install.sh") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("agenticsora.com","malwareaudit.com"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Capture the full ProcessCommandLine and decode the base64 blob to confirm the /curl/<token> endpoint; check for the follow-on zsh loader and a persistence line appended to ~/.zshrc. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the Mac, block agenticsora[.]com and malwareaudit[.]com at DNS/proxy, and kill the zsh/curl process tree. Treat all local secrets as compromised. 3) HUNT: On the host look for ~/.local/.mpwd, /tmp/osalogging.zip, LaunchAgents at ~/.local/com.apple.<hex>.hcpi.plist, and outbound to 85.206.161[.]241:8443; sweep other Macs for the same domains and Terminal-spawned curl|zsh.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("curl", "zsh", "sh", "bash")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("agenticsora.com", "malwareaudit.com")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "curl" and ProcessCommandLine has "base64 -D" and ProcessCommandLine has "zsh")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceProcessEvents

| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MacSync server-side AppleScript stealer: osascript, dscl authonly, keychain, ditto to /tmp/osalogging.zip AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts MacSync's stage-3 credential harvest: a server-side AppleScript pulled via curl '.../dynamic?txd=<token>' and run through osascript, password validation with 'dscl . authonly', Keychain Safe Storage extraction, and staging to /tmp/osalogging.zip via 'ditto -c -k'. Article-specific because it pins on the named staging archive, the authonly validation, and the osascript-from-curl chain. Rationale: Anchors on three verbatim MacSync artifacts from Huntress — the '.../dynamic?txd=' AppleScript fetch piped to osascript, 'dscl . authonly' password validation, and the '/tmp/osalogging.zip' ditto archive — none of which are typical of benign macOS admin activity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://www.itsecurityguru.org/2026/07/30/fake-claude-install-guide-delivers-six-stage-macos-stealer-and-rat-huntress-finds/
ATT&CKT1059.002 T1555.001 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate MDM/admin scripts calling 'dscl . authonly' to validate a local password (rare and usually not paired with curl-fed osascript)
  • Backup or migration tooling using 'ditto -c -k' to archive folders (won't target /tmp/osalogging.zip)
  • Developer running an internal AppleScript via osascript (no 'dynamic?txd=' curl source)
  • Security product self-tests exercising Keychain access
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the osascript parent was a curl fetch to an attacker /dynamic endpoint; check whether /tmp/osalogging.zip, ~/.local/.mpwd, or /tmp/sync<rand>/ exist and were exfiltrated. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the Mac; rotate every credential class the stealer touches — macOS login/Keychain, browser-stored passwords, SSH keys, cloud/Kubernetes tokens, Telegram sessions. 3) HUNT: Look for the RAT LaunchAgent (~/.local/com.apple.<hex>.hcpi.plist) and C2 to 85.206.161[.]241:8443, and sweep the fleet for osascript spawned by curl and for 'dscl . authonly' invocations.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "osascript" and (ProcessCommandLine has "dynamic?txd=" or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "curl"))
    or (FileName =~ "dscl" and ProcessCommandLine has "authonly")
    or (FileName =~ "ditto" and ProcessCommandLine has "osalogging.zip")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

DeviceProcessEvents

    or (FileName =~ "dscl" and ProcessCommandLine has "authonly")
    or (FileName =~ "ditto" and ProcessCommandLine has "osalogging.zip")
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine

MacSync RAT C2 / wallet-exfil to 85.206.161.241 and agenticsora/malwareaudit infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts outbound connections to MacSync's confirmed infrastructure: the Mach-O RAT C2 at 85.206.161[.]241:8443 (TLS/WebSocket) and the delivery/exfil domains agenticsora[.]com, malwareaudit[.]com, main.sdhomeinspectors[.]com, main.southcarolinacounselor[.]com. Article-specific because it uses the exact IP and domains corroborated in the Huntress reversing. Rationale: Uses the verbatim RAT C2 IP 85.206.161[.]241:8443 and the seed-phrase exfil domains (main.sdhomeinspectors[.]com, main.southcarolinacounselor[.]com) from the Huntress analysis, all present in the article's pre-extracted IOC set — direct atomic indicators with near-zero benign overlap. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://cybersecuritynews.com/fake-claude-code-install-guide/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel or sandbox infrastructure in the org intentionally beaconing to the IOC for validation
  • A domain being sinkholed/reassigned to a benign parking host after takedown (verify current resolution)
  • Proxy/EDR log replay or backfill re-surfacing historical detonation traffic
  • Vulnerability scanners probing the exfil domains as part of an IOC-coverage test
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the InitiatingProcess making the connection (expect the MacSync Mach-O RAT under ~/.local); confirm bytes-out to 85.206.161[.]241:8443 and any POSTs to the /modules/wallets exfil paths. 2) CONTAIN: Block the IP and all four domains at egress, isolate the host, and remove the RAT LaunchAgent persistence. 3) HUNT: Reverse-search the fleet for any host that resolved or connected to these indicators, and for the stage-1 curl|zsh delivery and /tmp/osalogging.zip staging on those hosts.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "85.206.161.241"
    or RemoteUrl has_any ("agenticsora.com", "malwareaudit.com", "main.sdhomeinspectors.com", "main.southcarolinacounselor.com")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr == "85.206.161.241"
    or Url has_any ("agenticsora.com", "malwareaudit.com", "main.sdhomeinspectors.com", "main.southcarolinacounselor.com")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

MacSync wallet trojanization: app.asar swap + ad-hoc codesign of Ledger/Trezor apps AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts MacSync's stage-6 wallet tampering where installed wallet apps (Ledger Wallet/Live, Trezor Suite) are rewritten in place by swapping app.asar, injecting recovery-step-*.html phishing pages, and ad-hoc re-signing with 'codesign -f -s -'. Article-specific because it keys on modification of app.asar inside wallet bundles and the injected phishing filename pattern. Rationale: Targets the specific stage-6 artifacts Huntress documented — in-place app.asar replacement inside Ledger/Trezor bundles and injected 'recovery-step-*.html' seed-phrase phishing pages — a high-signal tamper pattern; medium FP because legitimate Electron wallet updates also rewrite app.asar, mitigated by the recovery-step filename and by pivoting on the writing process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/macsync-stealer-rat-reverse-engineering • https://gbhackers.com/fake-claude-code-installer-3/
ATT&CKT1554 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Ledger Live / Trezor Suite auto-update rewriting its own app.asar (excluded when the writer is not the official updater or when recovery-step-* pages appear)
  • A developer rebuilding an Electron wallet app locally
  • MDM-pushed wallet app reinstall
  • Backup software restoring a wallet app bundle
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("Ledger Live", "Trezor Suite", "Squirrel", "com.apple.installer") and FileName !startswith "recovery-step-")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the process that wrote app.asar / recovery-step-* — if it is not the vendor's signed updater, treat as malicious; check for a preceding 'codesign -f -s -' ad-hoc re-sign of the wallet bundle. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, quarantine the tampered wallet app, and warn the user NOT to enter seed phrases; assume any wallet accessed post-tamper is compromised and initiate fund migration to a clean wallet. 3) HUNT: Sweep for the injected recovery-step-* pages and POSTs to main.sdhomeinspectors[.]com / main.southcarolinacounselor[.]com /modules/wallets, plus the upstream curl|zsh MacSync delivery on the same host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified", "FileCreated")
| where (FileName =~ "app.asar" and FolderPath has_any ("Ledger", "Trezor"))
    or FileName startswith "recovery-step-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
DeviceFileEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified", "FileCreated")
| where (FileName =~ "app.asar" and FolderPath has_any ("Ledger", "Trezor"))
    or FileName startswith "recovery-step-"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host

    category: process_creation

status: experimental

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:

            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e") or SHA1 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e") or MD5 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e") or SHA1 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e") or MD5 in~ ("3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["3db8befc08dc02ab7a76b5193abd81653775e8f3ceac5864c7c2188b2dbd3c54", "3ae26ed89d3a1a140edc89ca78513aba2895789ed0d0f64cad6605b6f2347c7e", "78dea0693ac2d70bdf8be7588667a75910e43fd84397ad484e710e37369a30f7", "9c09c303fa058c2d3e179969bd58ca5523775ff2d310fb2f8266ac74cb21ee81", "071bd109208eb1080ef525b5be394244cec467c59ffef5b8782cfb5e4850401d", "31566a1df7070f30cb990aa5eab310c1d4e0266c8776e9438138e5438ec1cff8", "230dff4bf9442a951dcd6898b2110924969a20668c20a43e3ceed6fcef65963e"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
